title: Renal and bladder trauma
subtitle: Grade it, keep the kidney, find the rupture

sources.org: American Association for the Surgery of Trauma (AAST) (Kozar RA et al., Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery)
sources.title: Organ injury scaling 2018 update: spleen, liver, and kidney

sources.org: World Society of Emergency Surgery (WSES) and AAST (Coccolini F et al., World Journal of Emergency Surgery)
sources.title: Kidney and uro-trauma: WSES-AAST guidelines

red_flags.text: Haemodynamic instability with a flank injury, flank haematoma or visible haematuria.
Rapid deceleration injury (fall from height, high-speed collision) even without haematuria: renal pedicle injury may not bleed into the urine.
Penetrating injury to the flank, back or lower chest.
Pelvic fracture with visible haematuria: bladder injury until a cystogram says otherwise.
Inability to void, suprapubic pain, rising creatinine or urinary ascites after lower abdominal trauma: an intraperitoneal bladder rupture can be missed for days.

do_now.text: Primary survey and haemorrhage control first. The kidney is rarely the reason a trauma patient dies; the bleeding elsewhere often is.

In a stable patient with suspected renal injury (visible haematuria, non-visible haematuria with hypotension, or a significant deceleration or penetrating mechanism), obtain contrast-enhanced CT with an early and a delayed excretory phase.
Pelvic fracture with visible haematuria: CT or conventional cystography with active retrograde filling of the bladder. Passive filling by clamping the catheter misses ruptures.
Check the urethra before passing a catheter in pelvic trauma; suspected urethral injury needs a urethrogram or suprapubic diversion.

assess.text: Mechanism, haemodynamics and response to resuscitation decide the pathway more than the grade does.
Grade the renal injury on CT using the 2018 AAST scale: it incorporates active bleeding, pseudoaneurysm and arteriovenous fistula, and guides embolisation and follow-up.
Pre-existing renal disease, a solitary kidney, and the function of the contralateral kidney.
Renal function at baseline and on follow-up.

investigate.text: Contrast CT with delayed excretory images for renal injury; the delayed phase shows collecting system and ureteric injury.
Retrograde cystography (CT or fluoroscopic) with adequate distension for suspected bladder injury.
Unstable patient taken straight to laparotomy: a single-shot intravenous urogram on the table can confirm a functioning contralateral kidney before any nephrectomy.
Repeat imaging for high-grade injuries, fever, worsening flank pain, falling haemoglobin or persistent leak.

resuscitate.text: Damage control resuscitation with blood products for haemorrhagic shock per the trauma protocol.
Angioembolisation for active renal bleeding, pseudoaneurysm or arteriovenous fistula in a patient who responds to resuscitation.

definitive.text: Non-operative management for haemodynamically stable patients with renal injury of any grade, with bed rest, serial haemoglobin and observation in a monitored setting.

Renal exploration for persistent haemodynamic instability attributable to the kidney, or an expanding or pulsatile retroperitoneal haematoma at laparotomy; attempt reconstruction where the patient's condition allows.
Persistent urinary extravasation or urinoma: ureteric stent, with or without a percutaneous drain.

Uncomplicated extraperitoneal bladder rupture: catheter drainage. Repair it surgically if the bladder neck is involved, bone fragments are in the bladder wall, there is a rectal or vaginal injury, or the patient is undergoing open pelvic fixation.

escalate.text: Trauma team leader owns the patient; urology advises on the genitourinary injury.
Interventional radiology early for active renal bleeding in a responder.
Urology in theatre for any renal exploration: reconstruction is often possible in experienced hands.

notes: Most renal injuries, including many high-grade ones, heal without surgery. The skill is selecting the few that need intervention, and that selection is driven by physiology.
If you open Gerota's fascia in a bleeding patient without vascular control, you will usually lose the kidney. Explore only for the indications, and know there is a second kidney first.
Intraperitoneal bladder rupture presents late as urinary ascites and a rising creatinine from peritoneal reabsorption. It is not acute kidney injury; it is a hole.
